agenda.title: Welcome to Demo Night
agenda.description: Run of show, presentation order draw, and the judging criteria for the class vote. Fourteen weeks ago these were word problems — tonight they are decision systems with dollar signs.
bulletPoints: Format: 10 minutes per team — 8 to present, 2 for questions
Scoring dimensions: problem framing, modeling craft, quantified business impact
Every project must answer one question: how much money does this decision make or save?

agenda.title: Presentations — Round One
agenda.description: The first four teams take the floor. Ten minutes each: the real problem, the data, the model, the solution, and the recommendation an executive could act on tomorrow.
bulletPoints: Teams 1 through 4, ten minutes each with hard stops
Audience scores each team on the shared rubric between talks
Live demos encouraged — Colab notebooks ready, solvers warmed up

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Halftime. Compare notes, refill coffee, and let round-one teams exhale.

agenda.title: Presentations — Round Two
agenda.description: The final three teams present. Same rules, same stakes: a real decision, a working model, and a bottom line in dollars.
bulletPoints: Teams 5 through 7, ten minutes each with hard stops
Final rubric scores submitted as each team closes
Q&A pushes on the sensitivity question: what happens when the world shifts?

agenda.title: The Edelman of ISOM-839: Awards & Retrospective
agenda.description: The class votes for the best project of the semester — our own Franz Edelman Award — followed by a rapid-fire retrospective on what fourteen weeks of prescriptive analytics actually changed.
bulletPoints: Ballots in: the Edelman of ISOM-839 goes to one team
Lightning retrospective: the model, moment, or mistake that taught you the most
From Session 1's first LP to tonight's decision systems — the distance traveled

activities.title: Judge, Vote, Crown: The Edelman of ISOM-839
activities.description: You are the judging panel tonight. Score every presentation on a shared rubric, then cast a final ballot for the semester's best project — and, in true course fashion, let a few lines of Python tally the decision.

steps.title: Score each presentation
steps.description: Rate every team 1-5 on three dimensions as they present: problem framing (is it a real decision?), modeling craft (is the model right-sized and sound?), and business impact (are the dollars credible?).

steps.title: Ask one hard question
steps.description: Each student asks at least one question during Q&A across the night — the sensitivity, feasibility, or deployment question an executive would ask.

steps.title: Cast your ballot
steps.description: Submit one vote for the project you would fund tomorrow if it were your budget. You may not vote for your own team.

steps.title: Crown the winner
steps.description: We tally the ballots live on screen and award the Edelman of ISOM-839 — bragging rights in perpetuity.

codeBlock.code:
from collections import Counter

# One last decision model for the road: aggregate the class ballots
ballots = ["Team 3", "Team 1", "Team 3", "Team 6", "Team 3", "Team 1", ...]

tally = Counter(ballots)
for team, votes in tally.most_common():
    print(f"{team}: {'#' * votes}  ({votes} votes)")

winner, count = tally.most_common(1)[0]
print(f"\nThe Edelman of ISOM-839 goes to... {winner}!")

activities.discussionNote: After the crown is placed, close the loop: notice that every winning presentation led with the decision and the dollars, not the algorithm. That is the discipline to carry into every analytics job — executives fund decisions, not models.

takeaways.text: You just did the whole thing: real problem, real data, real model, real recommendation, real dollars. That end-to-end arc is the rarest skill in analytics — and now it is yours.

The market is waiting: BLS projects 12% growth for operations research analysts, and decision scientists average around $156K. Your free Gurobi Young Professionals license keeps the toolkit in your hands.
From the first LP in Session 1 to RL and LLM copilots at the frontier — you no longer just analyze what happened. You prescribe what to do next. Congratulations.
